scams.name: The Kuromon Market Tourist-Tier Overcharge
scams.description: Vendors at Kuromon Market systematically overcharge foreign tourists for seafood and wagyu. Prices are hidden, displayed only in foreign currencies, or obscured behind secondary signs. A 2024 investigation documented ¥30,000 for four crab legs and ¥3,500 for a single shrimp, though prices moderated after market association intervention. About 25 of 150 stalls carry the overcharging reputation.
scams.avoidance: Ask exact total price in Japanese before ordering and walk away if staff dodge the question. Eat at Tenjinbashisuji Shopping Street or standalone sushi restaurants on Tabelog instead. Photograph price signs before ordering. Verify the shop displays the association's fair-price flyer.

scams.name: The Dotonbori Wagyu Hamburger Bait-and-Switch
scams.description: Street hustlers lure tourists into unmarked restaurants with laminated menus advertising A5 wagyu. Once seated, staff claim card-only payment via portable readers with no cash register. Cold, poor-quality meat arrives and the bill—around ¥29,568—is already processed. October 2025 Reddit post documenting this drew 800+ upvotes confirming the pattern.
scams.avoidance: Never follow street hustlers in Dotonbori. Pre-select wagyu restaurants on Tabelog with 4.0+ stars and 100+ Japanese reviews. Legitimate places have visible cash registers and published prices. If trapped, stand and leave before ordering; staff cannot legally force payment without an order.
scams.location: Dotonbori and side streets off Shinsaibashi-suji, Chuo-ku

scams.name: The Minami / Kitashinchi Girls-Bar Bottakuri
scams.description: Hustlers offer girls bars at ¥3,000 per hour. Bills escalate to ¥300,000–¥950,000 after staff pressure customers to order expensive champagne bottles (¥200,000+). Door staff block exits; ATM withdrawal is 'suggested.' A January 2025 Suita case involved ¥950,000 charges and a January 2019 case resulted in police arrest after customers were beaten over payment disputes.
scams.avoidance: Never enter bars recruited from the street. Book Tabelog-listed venues with published prices and 20+ Japanese reviews. Leave before accepting food or drink if no menu appears. Say '警察を呼んでください' (call police) and dial 110 if challenged. Never let staff accompany you to ATMs.

scams.name: The Midosuji Line Panhandle Approach
scams.description: You're on the Midosuji Line between Namba and Umeda and a well-dressed young man sits next to you. 'Sorry, can I practice my English?' Two minutes later the story lands: his wallet was stolen at Kansai Airport, his hotel won't let him in without ID, the police 'can't help foreigners,' and he just needs ¥5,000 to ¥10,000 for cab fare home. A July 2025 Reddit thread documented the exact script, and a nearby Japanese commuter in the same thread confirmed the operator had been working the Midosuji Line for months — tourists see the sequence once, but he runs it many times a day.
scams.avoidance: Genuine Japanese homeless almost never approach strangers, and genuinely stranded tourists go to the koban outside every major Osaka Metro station (there's one at the south exit of Namba Station and one at the north exit of Umeda Station). If a stranger on the train opens with 'can I practice my English?' and the conversation turns to money in under three minutes, stand up at the next stop, walk off, and don't explain yourself. If they follow you off the train, walk straight into the station koban — which will end the approach instantly.
scams.location: Osaka Metro Midosuji Line (Namba↔Daikokucho), Shin-Osaka Shinkansen concourse, Osaka/Umeda station exits

scams.name: The Kansai / Itami Airport Unofficial 'Shirotaku' Taxi
scams.description: Suited men approach in arrivals offering 'flat-rate' taxi service bypassing official queues. White license plates indicate unauthorized shiro-taku drivers. Initial quotes (¥8,000) inflate to ¥15,000–¥32,000 with surprise tolls and night-service fees. A 2024 case charged ¥11,640 on a ¥3,000 route; another saw ¥32,000 versus the legal ¥20,000–¥22,000 fixed rate.
scams.avoidance: Walk directly to official taxi ranks—ignore anyone approaching in arrivals. Take Nankai Rapi:t (¥1,450) or JR Kansai-Airport Rapid (¥1,210) instead. Check that license plates are green (緑ナンバー)—white plates mean the driver is unlicensed. Photograph receipt, plate, and driver ID if charged unexpectedly and file a Kansai Transport Bureau complaint.
scams.location: Kansai International Airport (KIX) arrivals, Itami (ITM) arrivals, Shin-Osaka taxi overflow

scams.name: The Shinsaibashi / Amemura Counterfeit-Brand Shops
scams.description: Luxury items (Louis Vuitton wallets at ¥8,000, Moncler jackets at ¥15,000) sold from back-street shops are counterfeit. A 2024 Mainichi investigation documented the Tsuruhashi area nicknamed '鶴橋偽ブランド通り' where sellers ask 'You're not the police, right?' before revealing stock. Osaka Customs blocked ~9,600 counterfeits in FY2024; Japanese counterfeiting carries 10-year prison and ~$73,000 USD fines.
scams.avoidance: Prices 10–20% below retail are counterfeit. Buy only from official boutiques or major department stores (Hankyu, Daimaru, Takashimaya). Use secondhand authenticators with 50+ Japanese reviews (Komehyo, RagTag). Avoid Expo 2025 Myaku-Myaku merchandise from unofficial stalls. Do not export counterfeits—customs in EU, UK, US, Australia, South Korea will seize goods and levy fines.
scams.location: Shinsaibashi-suji, Amerikamura (Amemura), Tsuruhashi district in Ikuno-ku

scams.name: The Post-Expo 2025 Ticket and Myaku-Myaku Merchandise Fraud
scams.description: Osaka Expo 2025 ran from April to October 2025 and drew over 28 million visitors. During the run, fake websites mimicked the official Expo site, harvested card details, and sold counterfeit tickets whose QR codes failed at the gates; a March 2025 Trend Micro report flagged multiple fraudulent domains, and NHK and the Expo Association issued repeated warnings through the summer. Since the Expo closed, the same operators have pivoted to selling counterfeit Myaku-Myaku mascot merchandise through look-alike shops. A typical victim is charged around ¥7,500 to ¥15,000 for a 'limited-edition' plush that either never arrives or arrives as a poor knockoff from a foreign warehouse.
scams.avoidance: Expo 2025 closed in October 2025—any site selling 'Expo tickets' in 2026 is a scam. Buy Myaku-Myaku merchandise only from official licensees (Osaka Tourism Bureau shops and major department stores such as Hankyu, Daimaru, or Takashimaya). Never click Expo-themed ads on social media. If you've already paid a suspicious site, file a chargeback with your card issuer within 60 days and report the site to the Consumer Affairs Agency hotline on 188.
scams.location: Online with in-person pickup/ticket-swap attempts near Yumeshima Expo site and Osaka Station

scams.name: The Dotonbori Pickpocket and Phone-Hold Distraction
scams.description: Thieves target dense crowds at Dotonbori's Ebisu Bridge Glico sign photo spot (500+ tourists) and Namba Walk. Phones in back pockets vanish; a classic distraction involves asking you to hold someone's phone while taking a photo—while distracted, an accomplice rifles your bag. A 2025 NTV report featured a 41-year-old serial thief rearrested after CCTV caught him stealing a ¥35,000 wallet from a backpack; he told police 'Japanese people are easy targets.'
scams.avoidance: Wear a cross-body bag with zipper forward or money belt under clothes. Never put valuables in back or open jacket pockets. At Glico Bridge, stand with back to wall, not in crowd center. Don't hand your phone to strangers—ask uniformed staff instead. On Midosuji Line during rush hour, wear backpack on front. Report theft to nearest koban immediately for insurance purposes.
scams.location: Dotonbori crowds, Namba Walk, Shin-Osaka Shinkansen platforms, Osaka Metro Midosuji Line rush hour, Nara Park
